question: How do I calculate the tension on each sling leg from the sling angle?

body.text:
Math (physics, not rule text), for equal legs sharing the load evenly: leg tension = (load weight ÷ number of legs carrying it) × load angle factor. With the angle measured from horizontal, factor = 1 ÷ sine of the angle. Without a calculator, use sling length ÷ vertical height.

Example: 10,000 lb on 2 legs at 60°. 5,000 × 1.155 = 5,775 lb per leg.
Check that tension against the sling's rated capacity for the way it is rigged. The rule:
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: What are the load angle factors for common sling angles?

body.text:
These are trigonometry, not rule text. Angles are from HORIZONTAL:
• 90° (vertical leg): 1.000
• 60°: 1.155
• 45°: 1.414
• 30°: 2.000

Multiply each leg's share of the load by the factor. Example: a 4,000 lb share at 45° puts 4,000 × 1.414 = 5,656 lb on that leg.
The resulting tension must stay within the sling's rating.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: Is the sling angle measured from horizontal or from vertical?

body.text: The federal definition allows either reference, so always confirm which one is being used.
Angle of loading is the inclination of a leg or branch of a sling measured from the horizontal or vertical plane as shown in Fig. N-184-5;

Math, not rule text: the two readings add up to 90°. So 60° from horizontal is 30° from vertical. Mixing them up can badly understate tension. A leg 30° from horizontal has a factor of 2.000. A leg 30° from vertical has a factor of 1.155.

question: How do I get the load angle factor if the angle is given from vertical?

body.text:
Math (not rule text): subtract the angle from 90° to get the angle from horizontal, then use that factor. Or compute 1 ÷ cosine of the angle from vertical.
• 30° from vertical = 60° from horizontal: 1.155
• 45° from vertical = 45° from horizontal: 1.414
• 60° from vertical = 30° from horizontal: 2.000
The rule's definition recognizes both reference planes.

question: How do I find sling tension without knowing the angle or using a calculator?

body.text:
Use length ÷ height (geometry, not rule text). L is the leg's straight-line length from the hook connection point to its load attachment. H is the vertical distance from that attachment's level up to the same hook point. Measure both along the same leg, in the same units. L ÷ H is the load angle factor.

Example: 12,000 lb on two equal legs sharing evenly, L = 15 ft, H = 10 ft. Factor = 1.5. Each leg: 6,000 × 1.5 = 9,000 lb.
Compare the result with the sling's rating.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: Why does sling tension go up as the sling gets flatter?

body.text:
Each leg must still hold up its share of the weight, but only the upward part of its pull does that. As the leg flattens, it must pull harder, and more of that pull goes sideways. This is physics, not rule text.

For a 5,000 lb share per leg, angles from horizontal:
• 90°: 5,000 lb
• 60°: 5,775 lb
• 45°: 7,070 lb
• 30°: 10,000 lb
• 15°: about 19,300 lb

The load weighs the same, yet a sling that was adequate near vertical can be overloaded when flat.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: Is there a minimum sling angle I can use?

body.text: The rule text used here (the 1910.184 definitions and paragraph (c)(4)) sets no minimum angle. It does prohibit overload, including overload caused by angle.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

Practice, not from this text: avoid angles below 30° from horizontal (more than 60° from vertical) unless the sling maker or a qualified person approves. At 30° each leg already carries double its share, and small angle errors change tension quickly. Also follow the sling's tag, manufacturer instructions, site rules and any other standards that apply to your job.

question: How much can two sling legs lift at a given angle if I know the single-leg vertical rating?

body.text:
Math for two identical legs, equal angles, even load sharing (not rule text): maximum load = 2 × single-leg vertical rating × sine of the angle from horizontal. This is the same as 2 × rating ÷ load angle factor.

With 5,000 lb per leg:
• 60°: about 8,660 lb
• 45°: about 7,070 lb
• 30°: 5,000 lb

This covers angle only. Practice: use the rating on the sling or assembly tag and apply any hitch or hardware reductions. Check shackles and attachment points too.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: How many legs do I count when figuring tension on a four-leg bridle?

body.text: A bridle has multiple legs gathered over the hook.
Bridle wire rope sling is a sling composed of multiple wire rope legs with the top ends gathered in a fitting that goes over the lifting hook.

Practice and physics, not from the rule: don't assume all four share equally. On a rigid load, small differences in leg length or pick-point position can leave two diagonal legs carrying most of the weight. Unless equal sharing is assured by the rigging design or a qualified person, figure the load on only two legs. An off-center load may need a leg-by-leg calculation, because even half per leg can be too low.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: How do I figure sling tension when the center of gravity is off center?

body.text:
Don't split the weight in half. The leg whose pick point is horizontally closer to the center of gravity (CG) takes more vertical load.

Physics, not rule text, for two legs with level pick points, hook directly over the CG, and CG in line between the picks:
• D1, D2 = horizontal distance from CG to picks 1 and 2
• Vertical share 1 = weight × D2 ÷ (D1 + D2)
• Tension 1 = share 1 × L1 ÷ H
Swap the numbers for leg 2. H is the height from pick level to the hook point.

Example: 10,000 lb, D1 = 3 ft, D2 = 7 ft. Vertical shares are 7,000 and 3,000 lb before applying each leg's L ÷ H.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: Does sling angle affect tension in a basket hitch?

body.text: Yes, when the basket's sides are angled. In a basket hitch the sling goes under the load with both ends up.
Basket hitch is a sling configuration whereby the sling is passed under the load and has both ends, end attachments, eyes or handles on the hook or a single master link.

Physics, not rule text, with both sides sharing evenly at equal angles: tension per side = (load ÷ 2) × load angle factor. For 8,000 lb: vertical sides carry 4,000 lb each; at 60° from horizontal, about 4,620 lb; at 45°, about 5,660 lb. Practice: check the tag's basket rating, then reduce for angle and any tight bend at the load.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: How long do two equal slings need to be to get a 60, 45, or 30 degree angle?

body.text:
Geometry, not rule text. For two equal legs, level pick points and hook centered between them, multiply the distance between picks by:
• 60° from horizontal: 1.0 (leg length equals the spread)
• 45°: about 0.71
• 30°: about 0.58

Example: picks 10 ft apart need legs of 10 ft for 60°, about 7.1 ft for 45°, or about 5.8 ft for 30°. Longer legs give a steeper angle and less tension, but need more headroom. Measure effective length to the hook connection point, including hardware in line with the leg.
Then verify leg tension against the rating.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: How much sideways (horizontal) force do angled slings put on the load?

body.text:
Physics, not rule text: horizontal force per leg = leg's vertical share × (horizontal run ÷ vertical height). It also equals leg tension × cosine of the angle from horizontal.

With a 5,000 lb vertical share:
• 60°: about 2,890 lb
• 45°: 5,000 lb
• 30°: about 8,660 lb

On a two-leg pick from separate points, this force pulls the pick points toward each other. Practice: check that the load and lifting points can take the angled pull and compression. Consider a spreader or lifting beam arrangement designed for the job.
This force is separate from leg tension, which must stay within the sling's rating.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: What factor do I use if my sling angle falls between the common angles?

body.text:
Math, not rule text: use sling length ÷ vertical height for the actual factor. Other reference values, from horizontal:
• 70°: 1.064
• 50°: 1.305
• 40°: 1.556
• 35°: 1.743

Practice: if you only have a short table, use the factor for the next LOWER angle from horizontal. For 52°, use 50° or, more conservatively, 45°. This overstates tension slightly instead of understating it. If angles are measured from vertical, go to the next HIGHER angle.
The actual loading must not exceed the rating.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

question: Is it a violation if sling angle pushes leg tension over rated capacity, even when the load weighs less than the rating?

body.text: Yes, if the sling is loaded beyond the rated capacity that applies to its configuration and angle. Load weight alone does not show how hard the sling is loaded.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.
The term is defined this way:
Rated capacity or working load limit is the maximum working load permitted by the provisions of this section.
Practice: compare like with like. Check calculated leg tension against a single-leg rating, or total load against an assembly rating for that exact angle. Don't apply the angle reduction twice.
